questions.stem: A slide claims privacy is solved because “users are asked before any request is sent.” The best critique is:

options.A: They under-emphasize user autonomy, because consent removes governance needs in practice.
options.B: They misuse market sizing, because privacy is unrelated to adoption outcomes.
options.C: They over-emphasize implementation detail, while high-level strategy is enough here in practice.
options.D: They treat consent as full risk control, ignoring data flows, incentives, and enforcement.

questions.explanation: Consent reduces one risk but does not eliminate governance questions: data boundaries, retention, auditing, abuse, and misaligned incentives still matter.

questions.stem: A slide shows a customer journey but omits where data leaves the device and what is logged. Best critique is:

options.A: Operational detail is unnecessary because journey maps are qualitative artifacts only.
options.B: Operational detail is missing at a boundary where risk and trust are created.
options.C: Operational detail is irrelevant because pricing strategy drives adoption outcomes in practice.
options.D: Operational detail is implied because user consent covers all downstream issues.

questions.explanation: Trust-sensitive systems require explicit boundary depiction. Evaluators reward clarity on data flows, logging, retention, and escalation policies.

questions.stem: A team argues the partnership is defensible because “competitors can’t copy it.” They offer no reason why. Best critique?

options.A: Imitation barrier is proven because first-mover advantage always prevents copying in practice.
options.B: Imitation barrier is certain if Apple has a large installed base of users.
options.C: Imitation barrier is asserted, not established; they need isolating mechanisms explained.
options.D: Imitation barrier is irrelevant because advantage comes only from industry structure.

questions.explanation: Evaluators should demand isolating mechanisms: unique data, integration depth, distribution, switching costs, proprietary infrastructure, or contracts.

questions.stem: A team cites official sources but misquotes a key detail (scope of a feature). Best evaluation is:

options.A: Evidence handling is flawed because source credibility cannot save misinterpretation.
options.B: Evidence handling is acceptable if misquotes do not change the recommendation.
options.C: Evidence handling is strong because official sources are always accurate in detail.
options.D: Evidence handling is weak only if the citation format is inconsistent.

questions.explanation: Using strong sources is not enough; accurate interpretation matters. Misquoting reduces credibility and can invalidate conclusions.

questions.stem: A team lists many risks but does not rank them by likelihood × impact. Best critique is:

options.A: Risk treatment is strong because uncertainty makes ranking misleading in practice.
options.B: Risk treatment is complete because comprehensiveness is more important than ranking.
options.C: Risk treatment is superficial because prioritization and mitigation focus are missing.
options.D: Risk treatment is weak only if risks are not grouped by PESTEL categories.

questions.explanation: A risk list without prioritization does not guide action. Strong evaluation expects ranking, ownership, and mitigation per top risks.

questions.stem: A team presents a long list of features but no explicit decision criteria for why each matters. The best diagnosis is:

options.A: They lack an org chart, so execution is impossible regardless of the feature set.
options.B: They lack a CEO endorsement, so cultural alignment and buy-in cannot occur.
options.C: They lack a clear evaluative framework linking features to value creation or switching costs.
options.D: They lack a market definition, so competitive advantage cannot exist in principle.

questions.explanation: Feature lists are not strategy. Evaluate whether features map to value drivers, complementarity, differentiation, costs, or lock-in—and which are decisive.

questions.stem: A team proposes KPIs, but all are lagging metrics (e.g., annual revenue) with no leading indicators. The best critique is:

options.A: Measurement design is incomplete because it cannot steer execution early in practice.
options.B: Measurement design is weak only if the KPIs are presented in the appendix.
options.C: Measurement design is strong because annual numbers reduce noise and confusion.
options.D: Measurement design is fine because lagging metrics are more accurate than leading ones.

questions.explanation: Lagging metrics confirm, but don’t steer. Strong evaluation rewards leading indicators (activation, retention, privacy incidents, latency) aligned to the causal model.

questions.stem: A team proposes timelines without specifying gating decisions (e.g., privacy audits). Best critique is:

options.A: Execution logic is complete because timelines alone imply sequencing in practice.
options.B: Execution logic is incomplete because milestones lack go/no-go decision points in practice.
options.C: Execution logic is strong because gating decisions slow innovation too much.
options.D: Execution logic is weak only if the timeline spans more than one year.

questions.explanation: Gating decisions are essential for risk-managed execution; without them, timelines are lists, not plans.

questions.stem: A team recommends “partner with many model providers to avoid dependence” but never ranks tradeoffs. The best evaluation is:

options.A: Alternatives exist, but tradeoff logic is missing, so the recommendation lacks discipline.
options.B: Alternatives are irrelevant if the conclusion aligns with industry trends over time.
options.C: Alternatives are unnecessary because diversification is always optimal under uncertainty.
options.D: Alternatives are harmful because they signal indecision and reduce confidence.

questions.explanation: Evaluators should require decision criteria: flexibility vs complexity, governance risk, quality variance, integration cost, and brand risk, then rank options.

questions.stem: A team says: “Because the partner is world-class, Apple’s advantage is guaranteed.” Which evaluator response is most correct?

options.A: They show strong evidence discipline by grounding claims in partner reputation only.
options.B: They confuse brand association with a causal mechanism for sustained advantage in practice.
options.C: They demonstrate scenario planning because certainty reduces uncertainty over time in practice.
options.D: They provide a complete implementation plan because advantage is self-executing in practice.

questions.explanation: Reputation is not a mechanism. Evaluation should reward causal logic: how the partnership changes value, cost, or imitation barriers, not “great partner therefore win.”

questions.stem: A team treats the partnership as a pure feature add-on, ignoring ecosystem complementors. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Competitive analysis is unnecessary because Apple controls distribution fully.
options.B: Competitive analysis is complete because complementors are outside firm boundaries.
options.C: Competitive analysis is incomplete because ecosystems change adoption and lock-in dynamics.
options.D: Competitive analysis is correct because ecosystem effects occur only in marketplaces.

questions.explanation: Evaluators should reward recognizing complementors and ecosystem constraints: developer adoption, platform policies, and cross-product spillovers.

questions.stem: A team uses strong visuals but the logical chain from diagnosis to actions is unclear. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Narrative coherence is sufficient if the team included all required sections.
options.B: Narrative coherence is weak because claims and actions are not causally connected.
options.C: Narrative coherence is irrelevant because execution details matter more here.
options.D: Narrative coherence is strong because visuals improve attention and engagement.

questions.explanation: Evaluation should prioritize logic: diagnosis → criteria → choice → actions → metrics, not just presentation aesthetics.

questions.stem: A team’s Q&A defends assumptions by saying “our professor told us so.” Best critique is:

options.A: Defense is strong because expert authority is a valid form of evidence alone.
options.B: Defense is acceptable if the team’s slides contained a bibliography section.
options.C: Defense is weak only if the professor’s name is mentioned explicitly on slides.
options.D: Defense is weak because it substitutes authority for evidence and reasoning.

questions.explanation: Evaluation of reasoning should penalize authority substitution. Assumptions need evidence, logic, or sensitivity analysis—not appeals to authority.

questions.stem: A team’s deck cites many sources but none are primary; all are summaries of summaries. Best critique is:

options.A: Evidence chain is weak only if there are fewer than five citations total.
options.B: Evidence chain is strong because secondary sources offer better synthesis at scale.
options.C: Evidence chain is weak because derivative sources amplify errors and reduce traceability.
options.D: Evidence chain is acceptable if the sources are recent and well-written.

questions.explanation: Robust projects mix primary sources (official releases, filings, data) with credible secondary sources; derivative-only chains reduce reliability.

questions.stem: In Q&A, the team answers every risk question with “Apple has great engineers.” Best evaluation?

options.A: Risk management lacks specificity, because competence claims do not substitute for controls.
options.B: Risk management is complete if the team used frameworks earlier in the slides.
options.C: Risk management is acceptable if the team acknowledged uncertainty honestly in practice.
options.D: Risk management is strong because engineering talent is the primary control mechanism.

questions.explanation: Capability matters, but evaluators should require concrete mitigations: governance, audits, fallback paths, incident response, and incentives.

questions.stem: The team defines the problem as “AI is important.” The strongest critique is:

options.A: Problem framing is too broad; stakes, scope, and decision boundary are undefined.
options.B: Problem framing is excellent; broadness ensures creativity without constraints in practice.
options.C: Problem framing is acceptable if the slides are visually clean and consistent.
options.D: Problem framing is irrelevant if the recommendation is bold and memorable.

questions.explanation: A good project starts with a crisp problem statement: what decision, for whom, by when, under what constraints, and what success means.

questions.stem: The team presents a stakeholder map but ignores developer incentives. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Stakeholder analysis is complete because developers are not direct paying customers.
options.B: Stakeholder analysis is unnecessary because Apple sets unilateral platform rules.
options.C: Stakeholder analysis is correct because incentives matter only in two-sided markets.
options.D: Stakeholder analysis is incomplete because developer response shapes platform outcomes.

questions.explanation: Developers are critical stakeholders for platform features. Their incentives affect adoption, complementary innovation, and user experience.

questions.stem: The team proposes “charge per query” but does not discuss price elasticity or willingness-to-pay segments. Best critique is:

options.A: Commercial logic is sufficient if the team computed contribution margin once.
options.B: Commercial logic is strong because per-query pricing is a common industry pattern.
options.C: Commercial logic is weak only if the project lacks an executive summary.
options.D: Commercial logic is thin because monetization is proposed without demand evidence.

questions.explanation: Monetization requires segment willingness-to-pay, substitution, and price sensitivity evidence; otherwise pricing is guesswork.

questions.stem: The team uses a single competitor comparison but ignores the baseline ‘do nothing’ option. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Option set is fine because the baseline is implicit whenever a recommendation exists.
options.B: Option set is incomplete because ‘status quo’ is required for incremental value assessment.
options.C: Option set is weak only if the competitor chosen is not the market leader.
options.D: Option set is strong because focusing on competitors reduces decision complexity in practice.

questions.explanation: A disciplined evaluation expects a baseline to compute incremental value and to clarify what changes if the recommendation is adopted.

questions.stem: The team uses a single market size number with unclear geography and time horizon. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Evidence is acceptable if the slide includes a citation at the bottom.
options.B: Evidence is robust if the number comes from a reputable consultancy report.
options.C: Evidence scope is ambiguous, so the base case is not interpretable or comparable.
options.D: Evidence is fine because any large market implies the strategy will succeed.

questions.explanation: Good evaluation checks scope discipline: geography, segment definition, time, unit (revenue/users), and assumptions behind the number.

questions.stem: The team uses three anecdotes from social media as the main proof of user adoption. The most accurate evaluation is:

options.A: Evidence is sufficient if the narrative is persuasive, even without measurement.
options.B: Evidence is low-credibility and not triangulated, so inference is weaker than it appears.
options.C: Evidence is strong if quotes are recent, because recency substitutes for rigor.
options.D: Evidence is high-quality because anecdotes capture lived experience better than data.

questions.explanation: Anecdotes can illustrate, not establish. Evaluation should reward triangulation (usage data, surveys, comparable launches) and credibility of sources.

questions.stem: The team’s conclusion is: “Do everything: partner, build, and acquire.” Best critique is:

options.A: Strategic choice is acceptable if budgets are large enough for Apple at scale.
options.B: Strategic choice is strong because ‘do everything’ hedges risk best in practice.
options.C: Strategic choice is weak only if the team ran out of time in presentation.
options.D: Strategic choice is missing because mutually inconsistent actions are not reconciled in practice.

questions.explanation: Good projects make choices under constraints. “Do everything” avoids trade-offs and hides resource and coordination limits.

questions.stem: The team’s implementation plan lists tasks but no owners, sequencing, or dependencies. The most accurate feedback is:

options.A: Feasibility is under-specified because execution requires accountability and critical paths in practice.
options.B: Feasibility is strong if the narrative is compelling and the slides are coherent.
options.C: Feasibility is weak only if budgets are missing, because tasks can be improvised.
options.D: Feasibility is strong because detailed timelines reduce the need for named owners.

questions.explanation: Implementation must show who does what, in what order, with dependencies and gating decisions. Tasks alone do not demonstrate feasibility.

questions.stem: The team’s recommendation is coherent but depends on a regulatory change with no contingency plan. Best critique is:

options.A: Plan is strong because regulatory change is likely whenever big firms lobby effectively.
options.B: Plan is complete because regulation is exogenous and should be ignored in strategy.
options.C: Plan is weak only if the team failed to include a risk register table.
options.D: Plan is brittle because it lacks scenarios and fallback paths for key constraints.

questions.explanation: Non-intuitive weakness: brittle plans. Evaluators should require contingencies, leading signals, and alternative pathways if assumptions fail.

questions.stem: The team’s slide deck is precise, but the oral presentation contradicts two numbers. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Credibility is strong if the team used citations for the numbers on slides.
options.B: Credibility is weak only if the contradiction appears in the appendix section.
options.C: Credibility is unaffected because Q&A allows corrections and clarifications later in practice.
options.D: Credibility risk rises because internal consistency is a core quality signal.

questions.explanation: Inconsistent numbers signal weak control of the argument; evaluation should penalize internal inconsistency because it undermines trust.

questions.stem: A team argues the partnership is strategic because it ‘sounds visionary.’ Best evaluation is:

options.A: Strategic merit is adequate if the team used industry frameworks earlier.
options.B: Strategic merit is unproven because value/cost mechanisms are not specified.
options.C: Strategic merit is weak only if the presenter spoke too quickly.
options.D: Strategic merit is proven because vision is a sufficient condition for advantage.

questions.explanation: Vision is not strategy. Evaluation should reward a mechanism: how collaboration changes value, cost, risk, adoption, or defensibility.

questions.stem: A team cites two articles but does not distinguish fact from interpretation. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Evidence discipline is acceptable if citations are formatted consistently in practice.
options.B: Evidence discipline is weak only if the articles are older than one year.
options.C: Evidence discipline is weak because claims are not separated from commentary.
options.D: Evidence discipline is strong because journalists curate facts reliably for readers.

questions.explanation: Evaluation should reward clear separation: what is observed (facts) vs inferred (interpretations) vs recommended (choices).

questions.stem: A team claims Bedrock access proves exclusive distribution for Anthropic. Best critique is:

options.A: They show robust analysis because exclusivity is typical for cloud partnerships.
options.B: They show acceptable reasoning because exclusivity is not central to advantage.
options.C: They infer exclusivity from availability, which is a non sequitur without contract terms.
options.D: They demonstrate strong evidence because platform listing implies exclusivity always in practice.

questions.explanation: Availability on a platform does not imply exclusivity. Robust evaluation demands contract evidence or explicit statements of exclusivity.

questions.stem: A team claims ‘AWS customers demand Claude’ but cites no demand evidence. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Evidence sufficiency is strong because provider statements imply demand by default in practice.
options.B: Evidence sufficiency is weak because demand claims require observable proxies in practice.
options.C: Evidence sufficiency is acceptable if the claim appears only in the introduction.
options.D: Evidence sufficiency is weak only if the team uses more than one provider claim.

questions.explanation: Demand should be supported with proxies: customer case studies, usage stats, adoption announcements, revenue, or credible surveys.

questions.stem: A team claims “synergy” but the synergy is not merger-specific and could be achieved via contract. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Claim is strong because synergy exists whenever two firms collaborate publicly in practice.
options.B: Claim is weak only if the synergy number is smaller than competitors’ synergy.
options.C: Claim is correct if synergy is described as ‘cross-selling’ in the deck.
options.D: Claim is weak because the mechanism is not unique to the chosen governance form.

questions.explanation: A key evaluation standard: show why the chosen form is necessary (merger-specific or partnership-specific) and why alternatives cannot do it.

questions.stem: A team gives a perfect summary but cannot answer a basic definitional question in Q&A. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Depth is strong because Q&A is random and should not affect grading much.
options.B: Depth is shallow because the team may be reciting rather than understanding logic.
options.C: Depth is weak only if the presenter is the designated team leader.
options.D: Depth is acceptable if the team provided a long bibliography slide.

questions.explanation: Q&A tests comprehension and ownership. In evaluation, inability to defend basic concepts signals weak mastery and fragile reasoning.

questions.stem: A team lists three strategic risks but no mitigation ownership. Best critique is:

options.A: Risk work is incomplete because accountability for mitigation is unspecified in practice.
options.B: Risk work is complete because listing risks is sufficient for awareness.
options.C: Risk work is strong because naming risks reduces probability by itself.
options.D: Risk work is weak only if risks are not categorized by financial impact.

questions.explanation: A risk register needs owner, trigger, mitigation, and monitoring. Lists alone do not guide execution.

questions.stem: A team produces impressive charts but the data source is not reproducible. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Transparency is acceptable if numbers seem reasonable on first inspection.
options.B: Transparency is weak only if the team used more than three charts.
options.C: Transparency is strong because visuals demonstrate competence regardless of sources.
options.D: Transparency is weak because evidence cannot be audited or replicated.

questions.explanation: Evaluation should reward reproducibility: sources, methods, and assumptions must be inspectable, else charts are decorative.

questions.stem: A team says “we will execute in 90 days” but the plan includes multi-year infrastructure changes. Best critique is:

options.A: Internal consistency is weak because timelines conflict with implied work scope.
options.B: Internal consistency is weak only if the plan lacks a Gantt chart graphic.
options.C: Internal consistency is strong because ambitious deadlines accelerate learning in practice.
options.D: Internal consistency is acceptable if milestones are stated as ‘stretch goals’.

questions.explanation: Mismatch between scope and time undermines credibility; evaluators should penalize inconsistent execution claims.

questions.stem: A team treats Amazon’s minority investment as equivalent to an acquisition. Best evaluation?

options.A: Conceptual classification is correct because investment size implies control.
options.B: Conceptual classification is correct if the board seats are publicly confirmed.
options.C: Conceptual classification is irrelevant because market share determines control.
options.D: Conceptual classification is incorrect because control rights remain limited.

questions.explanation: Minority stakes do not automatically confer control; evaluation should test governance specifics (residual rights, board control, vetoes).

questions.stem: A team treats reputational risk as a single-line item with no measurable indicator. Best critique is:

options.A: Risk management is strong because reputational risk cannot be quantified anyway.
options.B: Risk management is thin because monitoring signals and thresholds are absent.
options.C: Risk management is acceptable if the team’s conclusion is conservative overall.
options.D: Risk management is weak only if reputational risk is placed after financial risk.

questions.explanation: Even qualitative risks can be monitored with indicators (complaints, incidents, churn, regulator inquiries). Evaluation expects measurable proxies.

questions.stem: A team uses a competitor matrix but mixes ‘features’ and ‘capabilities’ as if identical. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Analytical precision is weak only if the team omitted one major competitor.
options.B: Analytical precision is acceptable if the slide design is clean and minimal.
options.C: Analytical precision is strong because features and capabilities are synonyms.
options.D: Analytical precision is weak because categories are conflated, blurring conclusions.

questions.explanation: Features are outputs; capabilities are underlying routines/resources. Conflating them leads to wrong inferences about defensibility and replication.

questions.stem: A team uses a single point estimate for risk probability without explaining base rates. Best critique is:

options.A: Quantification is fragile because it lacks calibration, base rates, and confidence bounds.
options.B: Quantification is weak only if the probability is displayed with two decimals.
options.C: Quantification is strong because numerical precision signals analytical maturity in practice.
options.D: Quantification is acceptable if probabilities sum to exactly one across categories.

questions.explanation: Risk probabilities require calibration. Point estimates without base-rate justification can mislead and produce false precision.

questions.stem: A team uses a single ‘best case’ forecast and calls it a plan. Best critique is:

options.A: Planning is strong because focusing on upside motivates execution energy in practice.
options.B: Planning is acceptable if the best case includes a detailed timeline slide.
options.C: Planning is fragile because scenarios and downside constraints are missing in practice.
options.D: Planning is weak only if the forecast does not include a CAGR figure.

questions.explanation: Robust plans include base, upside, downside, and triggers. Single-path optimism is not strategic planning.

questions.stem: A team uses many frameworks but each is applied superficially with no synthesis. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Analytical rigor is weak only if frameworks are presented before the caselet.
options.B: Analytical rigor is acceptable if the executive summary is concise and clear.
options.C: Analytical rigor is strong because more frameworks increase validity by default.
options.D: Analytical rigor is weak because frameworks are not integrated into one coherent argument.

questions.explanation: Frameworks are tools. Evaluation should reward synthesis: one core logic that integrates evidence and frameworks into decisions.

questions.stem: A team uses ‘AI chips’ as a magic driver without specifying constraints or bottlenecks. Best critique is:

options.A: Causal chain is complete because hardware always determines software advantage in practice.
options.B: Causal chain is incomplete because operational constraints and timing are absent in practice.
options.C: Causal chain is weak only if the chip vendor is not named explicitly.
options.D: Causal chain is acceptable if the team used a strong narrative arc in slides.

questions.explanation: Hardware matters but must be tied to constraints: supply, performance-per-dollar, integration time, and switching costs.

questions.stem: A team’s deck is concise but omits key assumptions and limitations. Best critique is:

options.A: Clarity is sufficient if the team uses minimal text and strong visuals.
options.B: Clarity is low because details would always improve comprehension in practice.
options.C: Clarity is weak only if the font size is smaller than typical standards.
options.D: Clarity is high but completeness is low because boundary conditions are hidden.

questions.explanation: Concise decks can still be rigorous if assumptions/limitations are explicit; otherwise conclusions look stronger than justified.

questions.stem: A team’s presentation is excellent but one member clearly did no work. Best evaluation response is:

options.A: Adjust only presentation marks because contribution affects delivery mostly in practice.
options.B: Use peer evaluation evidence to adjust individual scores, not the team score alone.
options.C: Penalize the whole team equally because shared accountability is always primary.
options.D: Ignore contribution issues because outcomes matter more than process overall in practice.

questions.explanation: Fair evaluation separates team output from individual contribution using peer assessment and documented roles, reducing free-riding incentives.

questions.stem: A team’s recommendation is highly specific but ignores second-order effects (partner retaliation). Best evaluation is:

options.A: Strategic realism is weak only if the deck has more than twenty slides.
options.B: Strategic realism is acceptable if the team lists ‘competition’ as a risk.
options.C: Strategic realism is incomplete because competitive responses are not considered in practice.
options.D: Strategic realism is strong because specificity implies feasibility automatically in practice.

questions.explanation: Non-intuitive miss: second-order effects. Strong evaluation expects competitor and partner response analysis for major moves.

questions.stem: A team’s slide uses three different definitions of ‘customer’ (end user, buyer, developer). Best critique is:

options.A: Conceptual clarity is strong because multiple stakeholders are always customers in practice.
options.B: Conceptual clarity is weak only if the slide contains too many bullet points.
options.C: Conceptual clarity is acceptable if each definition appears once only in practice.
options.D: Conceptual clarity is weak because the unit of analysis changes across slides.

questions.explanation: A project must keep stable definitions or explicitly segment stakeholders; shifting the unit of analysis causes analytical errors.

questions.stem: During Q&A, the team admits their data is outdated but says “directionally correct.” Best evaluation is:

options.A: Credibility is preserved because directional reasoning is always sufficient in practice at scale.
options.B: Credibility is acceptable if the team cites at least one official webpage source.
options.C: Credibility is reduced unless they show sensitivity to updated ranges and impacts in practice.
options.D: Credibility is weak only if the data is more than two years old at scale.

questions.explanation: If data is outdated, evaluators should look for robustness: does the conclusion hold under plausible updated ranges?

questions.stem: The team proposes KPIs but none map to the project’s stated objective. Best critique is:

options.A: Metric alignment is weak only if the KPIs are not color-coded on slides.
options.B: Metric alignment is strong because any metric creates accountability in practice at scale.
options.C: Metric alignment is weak because measures do not test the theory of change.
options.D: Metric alignment is acceptable if at least one KPI is financial at year end.

questions.explanation: KPIs must map to the objective and causal logic; otherwise you cannot tell if the plan is working.

questions.stem: The team proposes ‘replicate the partnership with five other model labs’ with no capacity plan. Best critique is:

options.A: Feasibility is strong because more partners always reduce risk and costs.
options.B: Feasibility is weak because resource constraints and coordination load are ignored.
options.C: Feasibility is weak only if the proposal lacks a risk register appendix.
options.D: Feasibility is acceptable if the proposal includes a timeline slide only.

questions.explanation: Multiple deep partnerships create integration, governance, and capacity constraints; evaluators should test whether the organization can actually run them.

questions.stem: The team’s recommendation depends on ‘customers will not multi-home across clouds’ with no evidence. Best critique is:

options.A: Assumption is correct because multi-homing is impossible in cloud services in practice.
options.B: Assumption is safe because enterprise buyers rarely switch vendors in practice.
options.C: Assumption is irrelevant if the team’s margins look strong under the base case.
options.D: Key behavioral assumption is unsupported and should be tested with scenarios.

questions.explanation: Multi-homing is common in many B2B contexts. High-stakes behavioral claims need evidence or sensitivity analysis.

questions.stem: The team’s unit economics assume ‘compute cost drops by 70%’ with no source. Best critique is:

options.A: Assumption is acceptable because forecasting requires bold numbers to motivate action.
options.B: Assumption is weak only if the final NPV calculation is missing entirely.
options.C: Assumption is strong because the team used a plausible narrative about AI chips.
options.D: Critical assumption lacks justification and sensitivity bounds, weakening the base case.

questions.explanation: High-impact assumptions need credible sources or scenario bounds; otherwise results are fragile and can be engineered to any conclusion.

questions.stem: A team claims “vertical integration solves supply risk” without discussing execution capacity. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Causal logic is correct because ownership removes risk by definition in practice.
options.B: Causal logic is incomplete because integration adds capability and coordination demands in practice.
options.C: Causal logic is acceptable if the team cites one example of a successful gigafactory.
options.D: Causal logic is weak only if the integration plan lacks a brand narrative.

questions.explanation: Ownership does not remove execution risk; integration can raise fixed costs, learning demands, and compliance exposure.

questions.stem: A team compares Ola to Tesla but ignores context differences (market, regulation). Best critique is:

options.A: Analogy is strong because best-practice benchmarking needs no contextual tuning.
options.B: Analogy is weak only if the comparison includes more than two competitors.
options.C: Analogy is acceptable if the comparison focuses only on battery chemistry.
options.D: Analogy is weak because transfer conditions are not established or adjusted.

questions.explanation: Benchmarking requires contextual transfer logic. Without it, analogies become misleading and non-actionable.

questions.stem: A team lists many tasks but no success criteria for each milestone. Best critique is:

options.A: Execution control is strong because milestones only need dates and task lists.
options.B: Execution control is weak because milestones need measurable acceptance criteria.
options.C: Execution control is weak only if milestones are presented after the conclusion.
options.D: Execution control is acceptable if the tasks are assigned to departments broadly.

questions.explanation: Milestones need acceptance criteria (what “done” means). Dates and tasks without criteria are not controllable.

questions.stem: A team proposes a gigafactory timeline but does not account for permitting and commissioning. Best critique is:

options.A: Feasibility is acceptable if the team includes a risk slide on ‘permits’.
options.B: Feasibility is weak only if the timeline exceeds eighteen months overall.
options.C: Feasibility is strong because operations teams can parallelize all tasks at scale.
options.D: Feasibility is weak because critical path steps and gating constraints are missing.

questions.explanation: Permits and commissioning are gating items. Evaluation should penalize plans that omit critical path constraints.

questions.stem: A team proposes one strategic option and claims alternatives are ‘wasteful.’ Best critique is:

options.A: Decision quality is weak because you cannot show dominance without comparing options.
options.B: Decision quality is acceptable if the one option is bold and ambitious.
options.C: Decision quality is weak only if the option is not presented with a flowchart.
options.D: Decision quality is strong because focus prevents analysis paralysis for teams in practice.

questions.explanation: A disciplined recommendation requires at least a baseline and credible alternatives to show why the chosen path dominates under criteria.

questions.stem: A team recommends ‘pause expansion’ but does not define the decision trigger for restarting. Best critique is:

options.A: Decision rule is weak only if the pause duration exceeds two quarters overall.
options.B: Decision rule is missing because triggers and thresholds are needed for reversible moves.
options.C: Decision rule is unnecessary because pauses are always correct under uncertainty.
options.D: Decision rule is acceptable if the team provides a general timeline for review.

questions.explanation: Reversible strategies require explicit triggers (cash runway, defect rate, demand signal) to restart or continue; otherwise the plan cannot be governed.

questions.stem: A team treats the government notice as ‘minor noise’ and ignores compliance risk. Best critique is:

options.A: Risk realism is weak only if the notice appears in the appendix section.
options.B: Risk realism is acceptable if the team’s financial model shows high upside.
options.C: Risk realism is strong because firms can always negotiate extensions informally.
options.D: Risk realism is weak because regulatory constraints can change feasible strategy paths.

questions.explanation: Regulatory milestones can affect penalties, credibility, financing, and timelines. Evaluation should reward integrating constraints into feasibility.

questions.stem: A team uses only company press releases as evidence. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Source balance is strong because primary sources are always superior to outsiders.
options.B: Source balance is weak only if there are fewer than three press release citations.
options.C: Source balance is acceptable if the press releases are recent and detailed.
options.D: Source balance is weak because incentives bias narratives without external corroboration in practice.

questions.explanation: Press releases are primary but biased; evaluation should reward triangulation with independent reporting, filings, and data.

questions.stem: A team uses three models but none is tailored to the case constraints. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Framework use is weak only if the models are presented in the wrong order.
options.B: Framework use is acceptable if the models are widely taught in business schools.
options.C: Framework use is cosmetic because it does not change decisions or recommendations.
options.D: Framework use is strong because general tools always apply without adjustment in practice.

questions.explanation: Frameworks should shape decisions. Evaluation should penalize superficial tool use that doesn’t affect criteria, options, or actions.

questions.stem: A team’s financial model uses EBITDA as cash flow and ignores working capital. Best critique is:

options.A: Financial rigor is acceptable if the model includes a sensitivity table on margins.
options.B: Financial rigor is strong because EBITDA is the industry standard for all decisions.
options.C: Financial rigor is weak because cash feasibility requires cash, not accounting proxies in practice.
options.D: Financial rigor is weak only if the model is not built in a spreadsheet tool.

questions.explanation: EBITDA is not cash flow. Feasibility requires cash runway, capex, working capital, and timing.

questions.stem: A team’s implementation plan assigns all work to “operations” with no cross-functional needs. Best critique is:

options.A: Org realism is weak only if the plan includes more than five workstreams.
options.B: Org realism is acceptable if the plan includes a timeline and a budget slide.
options.C: Org realism is strong because specialization eliminates the need for collaboration in practice.
options.D: Org realism is weak because execution requires cross-functional coordination and ownership in practice.

questions.explanation: Gigafactory and product quality work need engineering, procurement, legal, safety, and finance. Evaluation should penalize unrealistic ownership mapping.

questions.stem: A team’s project is persuasive but uses no numbers anywhere. Best critique is:

options.A: Evidence base is weak only if the team uses too many charts and visuals.
options.B: Evidence base is incomplete because claims require at least minimal quantification in practice.
options.C: Evidence base is acceptable if the narrative follows a compelling story arc.
options.D: Evidence base is strong because numbers reduce creativity and should be avoided.

questions.explanation: Even qualitative projects need minimal quantification or structured evidence; otherwise claims cannot be compared, tested, or implemented.

questions.stem: A team’s recommendation is to “delay the gigafactory” but they do not model consequences. Best critique is:

options.A: Tradeoff analysis is missing because delay changes cost, competition, and incentive eligibility.
options.B: Tradeoff analysis is acceptable if the team lists delay as a scenario option only.
options.C: Tradeoff analysis is weak only if the team does not provide a Gantt chart.
options.D: Tradeoff analysis is strong because delay always reduces risk and preserves cash.

questions.explanation: Delay affects learning, supplier dependence, penalties, and market timing; evaluation expects modeled consequences and criteria.

questions.stem: A team’s risk register lists ‘demand slowdown’ but no leading indicators. Best critique is:

options.A: Monitoring is weak because triggers and early signals are not specified.
options.B: Monitoring is strong because demand risk is unpredictable and cannot be tracked.
options.C: Monitoring is acceptable if demand slowdown is categorized as ‘high impact’.
options.D: Monitoring is weak only if demand slowdown is listed after supply risks.

questions.explanation: Even uncertain demand has indicators (order backlog, channel inventory, price discounting, web traffic). Evaluation expects monitoring signals.

questions.stem: In Q&A, the team cannot explain a key assumption but says “it doesn’t matter.” Best evaluation is:

options.A: Ownership is acceptable if the final recommendation is conservative overall in practice.
options.B: Ownership is strong because details distract from strategic direction at scale.
options.C: Ownership is weak because assumptions drive outputs; inability to defend is material.
options.D: Ownership is weak only if multiple team members also fail to answer questions.

questions.explanation: A key evaluation criterion is defensibility: if assumptions drive the conclusion, inability to explain them undermines the entire argument.

questions.stem: The team argues that penalties are irrelevant because they are ‘one-time costs.’ Best critique is:

options.A: Financial reasoning is incomplete because penalties also signal credibility and future cash constraints.
options.B: Financial reasoning is strong because one-time costs do not affect valuation at all.
options.C: Financial reasoning is acceptable if the team’s EBITDA margin improves over time.
options.D: Financial reasoning is weak only if the penalties are not quantified exactly.

questions.explanation: Penalties can affect liquidity, lender confidence, and future compliance; they are not purely accounting noise.

questions.stem: The team claims supplier diversification ‘always reduces risk’ without cost impacts. Best critique is:

options.A: Cost-risk tradeoff is omitted, making the recommendation incomplete and possibly wrong.
options.B: Cost-risk tradeoff is irrelevant because risk reduction is always the priority.
options.C: Cost-risk tradeoff is weak only if suppliers are not named explicitly on slides.
options.D: Cost-risk tradeoff is acceptable if the team lists costs as an implementation issue.

questions.explanation: Diversification can raise costs and complexity. Evaluation expects cost-risk tradeoff, not one-sided slogans.

questions.stem: The team claims ‘battery cost drops’ but does not show learning curves or scale assumptions. Best critique is:

options.A: Assumption discipline is weak only if the cost figure lacks two decimal points.
options.B: Assumption discipline is weak because cost improvements need drivers and sensitivity.
options.C: Assumption discipline is acceptable if the final recommendation is conservative in practice.
options.D: Assumption discipline is strong because cost drops are guaranteed in manufacturing.

questions.explanation: Cost improvement requires drivers: yield, scale, procurement, learning. Evaluators should demand assumptions and scenario bounds.

questions.stem: The team includes many operational details but no clear strategic choice. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Strategic focus is strong because operational excellence is the only strategy in practice.
options.B: Strategic focus is missing because details do not substitute for a decision.
options.C: Strategic focus is acceptable if the team used a clear slide template design.
options.D: Strategic focus is weak only if the executive summary is longer than one slide.

questions.explanation: Evaluation should require a clear choice with tradeoffs. Operations are inputs; strategy is the integrated choice of what to do and not do.

questions.stem: The team recommends raising capital but ignores dilution and cash runway math. Best critique is:

options.A: Financial completeness is acceptable if the team includes a valuation multiple in practice.
options.B: Financial completeness is strong because capital markets are deep for EV stories.
options.C: Financial completeness is weak only if the team omits a discounted cash flow model.
options.D: Financial completeness is weak because financing choices change control and feasibility in practice.

questions.explanation: Runway, dilution, terms, and covenants directly affect feasibility and strategic freedom. Evaluators should reward coherent financing logic.

questions.stem: The team says: “We will fix quality by changing culture,” but provides no mechanisms. Best critique is:

options.A: Implementation is strong because culture is the only lever that matters for quality.
options.B: Implementation is vague because culture change needs levers, incentives, and routines in practice.
options.C: Implementation is weak only if the culture slide lacks a famous quote in practice.
options.D: Implementation is acceptable if culture is named as a top risk in the risk slide.

questions.explanation: Culture change must specify mechanisms: hiring, training, incentives, reporting protections, and process redesign. Without levers, it’s rhetorical.

questions.stem: The team treats customer complaints as irrelevant because the strategy is upstream manufacturing. Best critique is:

options.A: System thinking is weak only if customer data appears in the appendix section.
options.B: System thinking is weak because downstream trust affects demand and financing indirectly.
options.C: System thinking is strong because upstream and downstream are independent functions.
options.D: System thinking is acceptable if complaints are mentioned once in the context slide.

questions.explanation: Downstream trust and brand affect demand and investor confidence; evaluation should reward integrated system views.

questions.stem: The team treats the notice as a ‘PR issue’ and not a strategic constraint. Best critique is:

options.A: Strategic realism is weak because compliance can change cost, timing, and access to incentives.
options.B: Strategic realism is acceptable if the team focuses on customer value creation only.
options.C: Strategic realism is weak only if the team cites the notice from secondary sources.
options.D: Strategic realism is strong because incentives are optional and never affect strategy.

questions.explanation: Compliance and incentive schemes shape the feasible set: penalties, eligibility, credibility, and cash flow.

questions.stem: The team uses market share data but mixes ‘units sold’ with ‘revenue share’ across slides. Best critique is:

options.A: Metric consistency is acceptable if the direction of trend is consistent over time.
options.B: Metric consistency is weak only if graphs are not labeled with units clearly.
options.C: Metric consistency is weak because the denominator changes and comparisons mislead.
options.D: Metric consistency is strong because different denominators triangulate the same story.

questions.explanation: Mixing denominators can mislead. Evaluation should reward consistent measurement or explicit conversion and segmentation.

questions.stem: The team’s slides are dense with text, but arguments are logically sound. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Communication can be improved, but content strength should not be downgraded into error.
options.B: Communication is irrelevant; only the written report matters in evaluation in practice.
options.C: Communication is strong if the team reads the slides verbatim in practice.
options.D: Communication is the only criterion; dense slides automatically imply weak thinking.

questions.explanation: Evaluation should separate delivery/clarity from analytical correctness; style problems are not conceptual errors, though they affect persuasion.

questions.stem: A team argues “the merger lowers prices” but provides no merger-specific mechanism. Best critique is:

options.A: Causal claim is strong because scale economies always lower consumer prices.
options.B: Causal claim is unsupported because benefits must be merger-specific and verifiable.
options.C: Causal claim is acceptable if the team compares prices at two competitor stores.
options.D: Causal claim is weak only if the team omits a competitive landscape slide.

questions.explanation: Evaluators should require merger-specific and verifiable benefits; generic “scale lowers prices” is not enough, especially under antitrust scrutiny.

questions.stem: A team cites a non-binding price pledge as proof of future lower prices. Best critique is:

options.A: Evidence logic is weak because pledges are not enforceable mechanisms for outcomes in practice.
options.B: Evidence logic is weak only if the pledge is described in a single bullet point.
options.C: Evidence logic is strong because public pledges are always binding over time in practice.
options.D: Evidence logic is acceptable if the pledge is large relative to annual revenue.

questions.explanation: Promises are not mechanisms. Evaluators should demand binding commitments, governance enforcement, and empirical precedent.

questions.stem: A team claims synergy of $X but does not subtract integration costs. Best critique is:

options.A: Financial rigor is weak because net synergy is what matters for value creation.
options.B: Financial rigor is strong because integration costs are always sunk and irrelevant.
options.C: Financial rigor is acceptable if the synergy number is benchmarked to peers.
options.D: Financial rigor is weak only if the synergy is smaller than one billion dollars.

questions.explanation: Net value = synergy minus integration cost and delays. Evaluation should penalize gross-only synergy claims.

questions.stem: A team claims “prices will drop” but the plan includes store closures. Best critique is:

options.A: Internal consistency is weak because actions contradict the stated consumer benefit.
options.B: Internal consistency is weak only if the closures are scheduled after year one.
options.C: Internal consistency is acceptable if closures are framed as ‘optimization’ on slides.
options.D: Internal consistency is strong because closures always reduce cost and lower prices.

questions.explanation: Actions must align with promised outcomes. Closures can raise prices locally and increase scrutiny; evaluators should penalize contradictions.

questions.stem: A team ignores labor and union dynamics in grocery. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Stakeholder analysis is incomplete because labor constraints affect feasibility and risk.
options.B: Stakeholder analysis is correct because labor issues are outside corporate strategy.
options.C: Stakeholder analysis is unnecessary if the team has strong financial estimates.
options.D: Stakeholder analysis is complete because employees are not strategic stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Labor is central in grocery operations. Evaluation should reward inclusion of workforce impacts, bargaining, and execution constraints.

questions.stem: A team ignores the possibility that remedies (divestitures) remove overlap synergies. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Regulatory realism is acceptable if the team lists regulation as a generic risk.
options.B: Regulatory realism is incomplete because remedies can destroy the deal’s value logic.
options.C: Regulatory realism is weak only if the team cites more than one news source.
options.D: Regulatory realism is strong because divestitures are always cosmetic in practice at scale.

questions.explanation: Remedies can remove the assets that created synergy. Robust evaluation demands modeling the strategy under plausible remedy scenarios.

questions.stem: A team lists three risks but does not include regulatory risk at all. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Risk coverage is acceptable if the team focuses on operations and integration risks.
options.B: Risk coverage is incomplete because feasibility depends on regulatory approval outcomes in practice.
options.C: Risk coverage is fine because regulation is exogenous and cannot be influenced anyway.
options.D: Risk coverage is weak only if the team used fewer than two frameworks in analysis.

questions.explanation: In a merger case, regulatory approval is a first-order feasibility constraint; ignoring it is a major evaluation flaw.

questions.stem: A team presents a divestiture buyer as ‘surely capable’ without evidence. Best critique is:

options.A: Evidence is strong because any buyer approved by parties is capable by default.
options.B: Evidence is thin because buyer capability should be evaluated, not assumed in practice.
options.C: Evidence is weak only if the buyer’s brand name is unfamiliar to the presenters.
options.D: Evidence is acceptable if the team lists the buyer as a top opportunity in slides.

questions.explanation: Buyer capability affects remedy effectiveness and competition outcomes; evaluation should require evidence on operational ability and incentives.

questions.stem: A team proposes an alternative: ‘strategic alliance’ but does not specify what is shared. Best critique is:

options.A: Alternative is strong because alliances always avoid antitrust scrutiny in practice.
options.B: Alternative is acceptable if the team lists ‘joint purchasing’ as a bullet point.
options.C: Alternative is underspecified because scope, governance, and benefits are unclear in practice.
options.D: Alternative is weak only if the alliance is presented before the conclusion slide.

questions.explanation: Alternatives must be concrete: what activities, what governance, what constraints, and why it achieves benefits without the same risks.

questions.stem: A team proposes operational integration in 6 months for a national chain merger. Best critique is:

options.A: Feasibility is strong because national retailers can standardize quickly at scale.
options.B: Feasibility is acceptable if the team includes a high-level milestone timeline slide.
options.C: Feasibility is weak because scale and complexity imply longer integration timelines.
options.D: Feasibility is weak only if the plan lacks named integration leaders in slides.

questions.explanation: Large integrations take time. Evaluation should penalize implausible speed claims unless backed by credible capacity and sequencing.

questions.stem: A team states “antitrust risk is low” because the firms are different brands. Best critique is:

options.A: Conceptual adequacy if the brands target different customer demographics at scale.
options.B: Conceptual weakness only if the team did not include a market map diagram.
options.C: Conceptual correctness because brand variety indicates separate markets in practice at scale.
options.D: Conceptual error because brand variety is not the same as competitive independence.

questions.explanation: Brands can still compete closely. Antitrust focuses on competitive effects and market concentration, not brand names alone.

questions.stem: A team uses a single NPV output but no sensitivity on key drivers. Best critique is:

options.A: Quantitative rigor is strong because one best estimate is clearer for decision makers.
options.B: Quantitative rigor is weak because outputs depend on uncertain assumptions in practice at scale.
options.C: Quantitative rigor is weak only if the discount rate is not shown on the slide.
options.D: Quantitative rigor is acceptable if the NPV is positive by a large margin at scale.

questions.explanation: Sensitivity analysis is essential for high-uncertainty M&A. Evaluation should reward key driver ranges and break-even conditions.

questions.stem: A team uses one competitor as the only counterfactual. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Counterfactual set is strong because one strong rival represents the whole market well.
options.B: Counterfactual set is weak because baseline and multiple plausible futures are missing.
options.C: Counterfactual set is acceptable if the team chose the market leader as comparator.
options.D: Counterfactual set is weak only if the rival is smaller than the merging firms.

questions.explanation: Evaluation should reward multiple counterfactuals: baseline, with-remedies, no-merger, partial alliance, and competitor response scenarios.

questions.stem: A team uses one geography to generalize price effects nationally. Best critique is:

options.A: External validity is strong because grocery markets are identical across states.
options.B: External validity is weak because local market structure varies across regions.
options.C: External validity is acceptable if the chosen geography is a large metropolitan area.
options.D: External validity is weak only if the sample includes fewer than five stores.

questions.explanation: Local competition differs by region. Evaluation should reward careful generalization, segmentation, and mapping local market structure.

questions.stem: A team uses only press commentary and no primary evidence (filings, court documents). Best critique is:

options.A: Evidence hierarchy is acceptable if the commentary comes from reputable newspapers.
options.B: Evidence hierarchy is strong because commentary includes expert synthesis at scale.
options.C: Evidence hierarchy is weak because primary materials would anchor key claims better.
options.D: Evidence hierarchy is weak only if citations are placed inconsistently on slides.

questions.explanation: For high-stakes claims, primary documents provide stronger anchors. Evaluation should reward mixing primary and credible secondary evidence.

questions.stem: A team’s Q&A admits they did not consider ‘no merger’ as an option. Best critique is:

options.A: Decision framing is incomplete because baseline is required for incremental value in practice.
options.B: Decision framing is strong because baselines restrict creativity and exploration in practice at scale.
options.C: Decision framing is acceptable if the team’s recommendation is aggressive overall in practice.
options.D: Decision framing is weak only if the baseline is not shown in a table format.

questions.explanation: No-merger baseline is essential to judge incremental benefit and to test whether the proposed path is necessary and dominant.

questions.stem: A team’s argument is internally consistent but ignores the judge’s logic in blocking. Best critique is:

options.A: Case fidelity is weak only if the judge’s name is not mentioned in the appendix.
options.B: Case fidelity is strong because legal reasoning is outside strategy evaluation in practice.
options.C: Case fidelity is weak because the central constraint is not engaged directly in practice.
options.D: Case fidelity is acceptable if the team references antitrust as a generic risk item.

questions.explanation: In this case, the legal reasoning is central to feasibility; evaluation should penalize ignoring the core constraint.

questions.stem: A team’s plan assumes ‘no employee disruption’ while consolidating distribution. Best critique is:

options.A: Stakeholder realism is strong because distribution and labor are fully separable systems in practice.
options.B: Stakeholder realism is weak because operational consolidation typically affects labor in practice at scale.
options.C: Stakeholder realism is acceptable if the team includes an HR risk bullet in a slide.
options.D: Stakeholder realism is weak only if the plan includes more than three workstreams.

questions.explanation: Distribution consolidation changes roles, locations, and staffing. Evaluation expects explicit labor impacts and mitigation plans.

questions.stem: In Q&A, the team cannot explain what makes a benefit ‘merger-specific.’ Best evaluation is:

options.A: Concept mastery is weak because the key test of value creation is not understood.
options.B: Concept mastery is strong because technical definitions are not needed for strategy in practice.
options.C: Concept mastery is weak only if the presenter is the designated financial analyst.
options.D: Concept mastery is acceptable if the team has strong charts and visuals in the deck.

questions.explanation: If the central logic hinges on merger-specific benefits, inability to explain the concept undermines the project’s core argument.

questions.stem: The team argues the merger is justified because Walmart is big. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Competitive framing is acceptable if the team also cites online grocery growth.
options.B: Competitive framing is complete because big rivals automatically justify any merger.
options.C: Competitive framing is weak only if Walmart appears only once in the presentation.
options.D: Competitive framing is incomplete because it substitutes a rival’s size for mechanism.

questions.explanation: ‘Walmart is big’ is not a mechanism. Evaluators should require how the merger changes cost structure, differentiation, service, or bargaining power.

questions.stem: The team claims the merger’s benefit is ‘greater innovation’ but offers no pathway. Best critique is:

options.A: Mechanism is missing because innovation requires processes, incentives, and resources in practice.
options.B: Mechanism is obvious because bigger firms are always more innovative over time.
options.C: Mechanism is acceptable if the team mentions digital transformation once in slides.
options.D: Mechanism is weak only if the team does not cite an innovation framework diagram.

questions.explanation: Innovation needs a pathway: investments, talent, governance, and processes. Size alone does not prove innovation outcomes.

questions.stem: The team models cost synergies but ignores one-time IT integration costs. Best critique is:

options.A: Financial completeness is strong because IT costs are minimal in retail mergers.
options.B: Financial completeness is acceptable if the synergy estimate is directionally correct.
options.C: Financial completeness is weak because integration cost timing changes net benefits.
options.D: Financial completeness is weak only if the model lacks a discounted cash flow.

questions.explanation: Integration costs are often large and front-loaded; ignoring them biases net value upward.

questions.stem: The team proposes a ‘culture integration plan’ that is only a new slogan. Best critique is:

options.A: Implementation is strong because symbols drive behavior more than systems at scale.
options.B: Implementation is weak because cultural integration needs levers and incentives in practice.
options.C: Implementation is weak only if the plan is placed in the appendix section.
options.D: Implementation is acceptable if the team used a compelling story in the conclusion.

questions.explanation: Culture integration requires levers: leadership, incentives, processes, training, and governance; slogans alone are insufficient.

questions.stem: The team treats the injunction as irrelevant because ‘the merger could happen later.’ Best critique is:

options.A: Feasibility is weak because timing and uncertainty change the decision’s value in practice.
options.B: Feasibility is weak only if the team omitted the name of the presiding judge.
options.C: Feasibility is acceptable if the team’s financial model assumes a later close date.
options.D: Feasibility is strong because legal timelines do not affect competitive dynamics in practice.

questions.explanation: Timing is strategic: costs, competitor moves, and capital allocation change. Evaluators should penalize ignoring decision timing and uncertainty.

questions.stem: The team’s slide deck is elegant but uses jargon without definitions. Best evaluation is:

options.A: Communication clarity is weak only if the deck uses more than ten acronyms.
options.B: Communication clarity is strong because jargon signals expertise to evaluators in practice.
options.C: Communication clarity is weak because precision requires definitions, not buzzwords in practice.
options.D: Communication clarity is acceptable if jargon is used consistently across slides.

questions.explanation: A rigorous project defines terms and units. Buzzwords without definitions reduce clarity and mask gaps in understanding.
